title: Allocating a Fixed Sample Between Two Groups: Variance-Optimal Designs and the Direction of Small-Sample Confidence-Interval Failure
content: Background: When two groups are compared by the difference of their means, a 95% interval that fails tends to fail on one predictable side, set by the sign of the skewness balance Γ, the standardised third cumulant of the difference in sample means. Γ depends on how a fixed total sample is split between the groups, so the design itself can move the direction of failure. We asked whether variance-optimal (Neyman) allocation, allocation chosen to balance skewness, and allocation set from an internal pilot change that direction as Γ predicts, and at what efficiency cost. Methods: A simulation study with a plan, design table, code and analysis script registered before the main run compared six allocation rules (equal; Neyman; minimising |Γ|; minimising |Γ| within a 10% variance budget; and two rules set from a 10-per-group internal pilot) in 120 settings: eight pairs of population distributions, including opposed-skew pairs and normal controls, standard-deviation ratios 0.5, 1 and 2, and total sizes 20 to 200. Each of 508 runs used 10,000 datasets; Welch, Hsu and bootstrap-t intervals were computed on identical, nested datasets. Outcomes were the probabilities L and U that the interval lies entirely below or above the true difference, their difference, coverage and width. Results: The side of Welch failure followed sign(Γ) under every allocation in 147 of 149 determinate cells (98.7%). The budgeted skewness-balancing design reduced |L-U| relative to Neyman in 23 of 27 eligible settings and relative to equal allocation in 29 of 31, at most a 10% variance increase. Under opposed skew no allocation removed the direction (65 of 65 cells). |L-U| exceeded the total coverage error in all 193 cells with a determinate imbalance of at least 1 percentage point. The one risky prediction, that Neyman allocation reverses the direction for lognormal against exponential data, failed in all four settings: the heavy-tailed lognormal group delivered half or less of its first-order effect, so the neutral split lay elsewhere (post hoc). Pilot-based allocation made the imbalance worse than Neyman in 37 of 41 settings and lowered Welch coverage by a median of 2.02 to 2.58 percentage points (exploratory). Conclusions: Allocation moves the side on which small-sample intervals fail, and Γ predicts which way. Designing for direction usually costs little efficiency, but its calibration is unreliable when one group is very heavy-tailed, opposed skew cannot be designed away, and plug-in allocation from a small internal pilot is harmful. Studies should report both sides of noncoverage and treat the allocation as part of the inference.
